evidence.domain: Compared with 12 CFR 1024.17 and Appendix E. Matches: aggregate accounting, 1/6 cushion, low point = cushion, deficiency = negative balance per (b), shortage >= one month repaid over 12+ months per (f)(3)(ii), under one month in 30 days per (f)(3)(i), surplus >= $50 refunded within 30 days if current per (f)(2). An analyst would accept it with those stated limits.

verdict: Re-audit of the 2026-11-13 round-69 audit after fix PR #15569. Of its seven defects, PR #15569 closed four: the high one (deficiency is now a negative account balance per 12 CFR 1024.17(b), so a $540 shortage from a $500 balance collected over 6 months is flagged), the page's wrong deficiency definition, the tests that pinned it, and the unpinned thresholds (an Appendix E test and boundary tests now catch the three threshold mutants that survived before). Three were only written into README Known gaps and remain: the 'most in question' total double-counts (3,179.96 on the sample), a sub-one-month deficiency recovered at once is noted, and the bill-entry note contradicts itself. One new medium gap: an account with both a deficiency and a shortage is never tested against the 12-month rule. Every regulatory output recomputed against Appendix E and Reg X is now right, 53 tests pass and 5 of 6 core mutants are caught, so it meets the bar with those stated limits.
